name: Hydrogen
facts: The most abundant element in the universe.
The lightest element: a hydrogen atom is just one proton and one electron.
Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen (H2O).

name: Helium
facts: Helium was detected in the Sun's light before anyone found it on Earth.
It has the lowest boiling point of any element, about -269 °C.
Liquid helium cools the powerful magnets in MRI scanners.

name: Lithium
facts: The lightest metal: it is less dense than water.
Lithium powers the rechargeable batteries in phones and electric cars.
It is soft enough to cut with a knife and is stored under oil.

name: Beryllium
facts: Emeralds and aquamarine are gemstones that contain beryllium.
It is light and stiff, so the mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope are made of it.
Beryllium dust is toxic and must be handled carefully.

name: Boron
facts: Boron is added to glass to make heat-resistant borosilicate glass (like Pyrex).
Plants need small amounts of boron to grow.
Borax, a common cleaning mineral, contains boron.

name: Carbon
facts: All known life is built on carbon.
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon, arranged differently.
Carbon-14 is used to date ancient objects.

name: Nitrogen
facts: About 78% of Earth's atmosphere is nitrogen.
Liquid nitrogen is about -196 °C and is used to freeze things quickly.
Nitrogen is a key part of proteins and DNA.

name: Oxygen
facts: Oxygen makes up about 21% of the air we breathe.
It is the most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass.
Fire needs oxygen to burn.

name: Fluorine
facts: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so it reacts with almost everything.
Fluoride in toothpaste helps protect teeth from decay.
Non-stick Teflon coatings contain fluorine.

name: Neon
facts: Neon glows reddish-orange in glass signs when electricity passes through it.
Its name comes from the Greek word for 'new'.
It almost never forms compounds with other elements.

name: Sodium
facts: Sodium reacts violently with water.
Table salt is sodium chloride (NaCl).
Sodium gives a bright yellow color in a flame test.

name: Magnesium
facts: Magnesium burns with a brilliant white light, which is why it was used in old camera flashes.
It sits at the center of the chlorophyll molecule that plants use for photosynthesis.
Lightweight magnesium alloys are used in laptops and car parts.

name: Aluminium
facts: The most abundant metal in Earth's crust.
Aluminium can be recycled again and again without losing quality.
It was once so hard to produce that it was valued like a precious metal.

name: Silicon
facts: Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust.
Computer chips are made from ultra-pure silicon.
Ordinary sand is mostly silicon dioxide.

name: Phosphorus
facts: White phosphorus glows faintly in the dark.
Phosphorus is part of DNA and of ATP, the molecule that carries energy in cells.
It was discovered in 1669 by a German alchemist who was distilling urine.

name: Sulfur
facts: Pure sulfur is a bright yellow solid.
The smell of rotten eggs comes from a sulfur compound, hydrogen sulfide.
Sulfuric acid, made from sulfur, is one of the most widely produced industrial chemicals.

name: Chlorine
facts: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas that is poisonous on its own.
It is used to disinfect swimming pools and drinking water.
Combined with sodium it forms harmless table salt.

name: Argon
facts: Argon makes up almost 1% of Earth's atmosphere.
Its name comes from the Greek word for 'lazy' because it hardly reacts.
It fills many light bulbs and protects metal during welding.

name: Potassium
facts: Bananas are famous for being rich in potassium.
Potassium reacts vigorously with water and burns with a lilac flame.
Your nerves and muscles need potassium to work.

name: Calcium
facts: Calcium is the main mineral in your bones and teeth.
Limestone, chalk and marble are all calcium carbonate.
Calcium gives a brick-red color in a flame test.
